questions.knowledge_point: Determining Moments When a Force Has Zero Magnitude
questions.problem:
A body of mass $7\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=2{t}^{2}-16t+5$ meters per second.
Calculate the time at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude.
questions.worked_solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-16t+5) \\  & =4t-16\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4t-16 & =0 \\ 4t & =16 \\ t & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at $t=4\,\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
A body of mass $9\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons.
At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the velocity of the body is given by $v(t)=(t-4){e}^{-t}$ meters per second.
Calculate the time at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude.
questions.worked_solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration. 

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((t-4){e}^{-t}) \\  & ={e}^{-t}+(t-4)(-{e}^{-t}) \\  & =(5-t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(5-t){e}^{-t} & =0 \\ 5-t & =0 \\ t & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at $t=5\,\text{s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Force Acting on a Body Given Its Displacement
questions.worked_solution:
By Newton’s second law,

$$
F(t)=ma(t),
$$

where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|) \\  & =-\frac{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tan}⁡t) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =ma(t) \\  & =2\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡t \\  & =2{sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Force Acting on a Body Given Its Displacement
questions.worked_solution:
By Newton’s second law,

$$
F(t)=ma(t),
$$

where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration.

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[{({t}^{2}+1)}^{-1}] \\  & =-{({t}^{2}+1)}^{-2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force, in Newtons, is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =ma(t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [-\frac{2t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}] \\  & =-\frac{t}{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A body of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis under the action of a single force $F,$ measured in Newtons. At time $t\ge 0$ seconds, the position of the body is given by $s(t)=4{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}+12t+24$ meters.

Calculate the time ${t}_{∗}$ at which the force acting on the body has zero magnitude. Do not round the answer.

${t}_{∗}=$

{{field-1}} $\text{s}$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Newton’s second law

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F(t)$ is the force, $m$ is the mass, and $a(t)$ is the acceleration. 

To find the velocity $v(t),$ we differentiate the displacement $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(4{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}+12t+24) \\  & =12{t}^{2}-12t+12\end{aligned}
$$

To find the acceleration $a(t),$ we differentiate the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(12{t}^{2}-12t+12) \\  & =24t-12\end{aligned}
$$

Since the mass is always positive, the force has zero magnitude when the acceleration equals zero. So, we set $a(t)=0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}24t-12 & =0 \\ 24t & =12 \\ t & =\frac{12}{24} \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the force has zero magnitude at ${t}_{∗}=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}.$
